title: Breathless, Dizzy on Standing, Numb Hands / Think of Amyloid Before More Heart Failure Drugs

blocks.text: Breathless, Dizzy on Standing, Numb Hands / Think of Amyloid Before More Heart Failure Drugs

AMaC MRCP PACES · X-32 · Consultation · PACES Consultation (Station 5) · Skills A, B, C, D, E, F, G · 20 minutes (15 with the patient, then 5 of examiner questions; warning at 13 minutes) · Guidelines: ESC position statement on the diagnosis and treatment of cardiac amyloidosis (Eur Heart J 2021;42:1554-1568), key points summarised by the American College of Cardiology (April 2021); ACC key points on cardiac amyloidosis (November 2020); NICE TA984 Tafamidis for treating transthyretin amyloidosis with cardiomyopathy (published 19 June 2024); NICE TA1121 Acoramidis for treating transthyretin amyloidosis with cardiomyopathy (published 14 January 2026) · Related AMaC: Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy and dilated cardiomyopathy stations; this one tests an infiltrative cause of heart failure with preserved ejection fraction

Dear Doctor, a 77-year-old retired surveyor. Eight months of increasing breathlessness and ankle swelling, diagnosed as heart failure with preserved ejection fraction. He cannot tolerate heart failure tablets because his blood pressure drops, and he fell last week on standing. Please assess and advise.
The patient has consented to see you. Please take a history, perform a relevant examination and explain your assessment and plan to the patient.

sections.heading: 4. The Hook and the Examiner Trap

blocks.text: The Hook. Heart failure with preserved ejection fraction in an older man who cannot tolerate standard drugs and had both carpal tunnels released should raise cardiac amyloidosis. The marks come from the right tests to find which type.

The Examiner Trap. He fell on standing and his pressure is low. Candidates add heart failure drugs, or call it age. Pass: amyloid suspected, no pressure-lowering drugs, plasma cell tests, pyrophosphate scan, amyloid centre. Fail: more tablets.

rows: Think
Say
Do
Ask about breathlessness, swelling, dizziness on standing and falls, then carpal tunnel surgery, numbness, bowels and tablets.
"What stops you walking? Do you feel faint on standing? Any carpal tunnel operations, numb feet or bowel changes?"
Breathlessness; swelling; postural symptoms; falls; carpal tunnel; neuropathy; bowels; tablets; weight loss.
Check the lying and standing blood pressure, the neck veins, the heart, the abdomen and the tongue and skin.
"May I check your blood pressure lying and standing, your neck, heart, tummy, tongue and skin? Tell me if anything hurts."
Postural blood pressure; neck veins; heart sounds; lungs; liver; oedema; tongue; skin; cover him.
Explain that a protein may be stiffening his heart, why more tablets could make him worse and what tests come next.
"I think a protein is building up in your heart. I'd rather not add tablets that drop your pressure while we find out."
Blood and urine tests; scan; biopsy if needed; amyloid centre; diuretic care; falls; review.

blocks.text: High-performance is an AMaC teaching label, not an official grade. It shows what lifts a pass from adequate to convincing. Critical fail is an AMaC practice flag for an action that could harm the patient today; it is not an official automatic PACES fail.
Who you are: A 77-year-old retired surveyor. You are courteous, worn out and frightened of becoming a burden.
Opening line: "I get breathless doing nothing now, and the tablets they gave me just make me dizzy."
Volunteered: you fell last week when you stood up quickly.
Only if asked: you had both carpal tunnel operations a few years ago. Your feet tingle. Your bowels are erratic. You have lost a little weight.
Only if asked about tablets: you stopped the heart failure tablets because of the dizziness. You take a water tablet.
Hidden concern (only if asked what worries you): you are afraid of ending up in a home. Say: "My wife can't lift me if I fall."
Your questions, in your own words: "What's wrong with my heart?" "Why can't I take the tablets?" "Will I get worse?"
How you react: if given more tablets, you will not take them. If listened to and told what the tests will find, you agree. If offered options, you choose.

Findings, released when examined: breathless on talking; respiratory rate 20; pulse 82 regular; blood pressure lying 118/70 and standing 92/58; SpO2 95% on air; temperature 36.6 °C. Jugular venous pressure raised. Quiet heart sounds. Mild basal crackles. Ankle oedema. Tongue and skin normal. Reduced sensation in both feet.

Results, only when requested: echo: thick walls, small cavity, preserved ejection fraction. ECG: low voltage. Serum free light chains normal; serum and urine immunofixation show no monoclonal protein. Pyrophosphate scan: strongly positive. DNA sequencing: wild-type transthyretin.

Question ladder: 1. What do you suspect? (D, R4) Cardiac amyloidosis causing heart failure with preserved ejection fraction. 2. What are the red flags? (D, R2, R3) Bilateral carpal tunnel surgery, intolerance of heart failure drugs, postural hypotension, neuropathy, thick walls with low ECG voltage. 3. How do you tell AL from ATTR? (E, R5) Serum free light chains and serum and urine immunofixation first; a pyrophosphate scan with no monoclonal protein supports ATTR, and DNA sequencing gives the type; a monoclonal protein needs urgent haematology and biopsy. 4. Why avoid conventional heart failure drugs? (E, R6) Poorly tolerated; they lower pressure and cause falls. 5. What treatment exists for ATTR? (E, R6) Tafamidis (NICE TA984), acoramidis (NICE TA1121) or vutrisiran (NICE TA1115), started through an amyloid centre under the NHS commercial arrangement, plus supportive care.

Curveballs: He asks for a stronger water tablet: use with care, it may lower his pressure. He asks if it is cancer: AL is linked to plasma cell disorders, but his free light chains and immunofixation are normal and the scan points to ATTR. He faints in clinic: lie him flat, urgent review.

Fail performance
CANDIDATE: Stand up quickly. [R1 Fail] You're just getting old. [R2 Fail]
CANDIDATE: (Skips the standing pressure.) [R3 Fail] Hypertensive heart disease. [R4 Fail] A chest X-ray. [R5 Fail]
CANDIDATE: I'll add an ACE inhibitor and a beta-blocker. [R6 Fail] Nothing to worry about. [R7 Fail] Come back in a year. [R8 Fail]

Examiner note: Critical fail (AMaC practice flag, not an official automatic PACES fail): the examiner sees a red flag, more blood-pressure-lowering tablets in a man who falls on standing could cause a serious fall. No consent, no postural pressure, and amyloid missed.
Pass performance
CANDIDATE: I'm the registrar. May I check your blood pressure lying and standing, your neck, heart and tummy? I'll help you stand. Tell me if anything hurts. [R1 Pass]
CANDIDATE: Any carpal tunnel operations? Any numb feet or bowel change? Do you feel faint on standing? [R2 Pass]
PATIENT: Both carpal tunnels. My feet tingle. I fell last week.
CANDIDATE: (Examines.) A postural pressure drop, a raised neck vein, quiet heart sounds and ankle swelling. [R3 Pass]
CANDIDATE: I suspect cardiac amyloidosis, a protein stiffening your heart. [R4 Pass]
CANDIDATE: Blood and urine tests for a plasma cell disorder, an echo or cardiac MRI, and a nuclear pyrophosphate scan. [R5 Pass]
CANDIDATE: I won't add tablets that drop your pressure. I'll refer you to an amyloid centre. [R6 Pass]
CANDIDATE: What worries you most? [R7 Pass]
PATIENT: Ending up in a home.
CANDIDATE: That is a fair fear; we'll plan around falls. [R7 Pass] Shall we arrange the blood and urine tests this week and the scans soon after? [R8 Pass]
Examiner note: Suspected amyloid, avoided harmful drugs and arranged tests. Did not name the types, DNA sequencing, tafamidis or a written plan.
High-performance performance
CANDIDATE: I'm the registrar. May I examine you? Would you like a chaperone? Please sit while we talk. [R1 High]
CANDIDATE: Any weight loss, family history or a past blood disorder? [R2 High]
CANDIDATE: (Examines.) A normal tongue, no bruising around the eyes, and reduced foot sensation. [R3 High]
CANDIDATE: AL or transthyretin amyloid; hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, constriction and sarcoidosis fit less. [R4 High]
CANDIDATE: AL needs a biopsy; transthyretin amyloid shows on the scan, then DNA sequencing gives the type. [R5 High]
CANDIDATE: Tafamidis, acoramidis or vutrisiran is for transthyretin amyloid, through the amyloid centre; meanwhile salt restriction, stockings and a falls assessment. [R6 High]
CANDIDATE: We'll involve your wife in planning. [R7 High]
CANDIDATE: I'll give you a written plan and a review date. [R8 High]
Examiner note: Added a chaperone, other causes, AL and ATTR testing, tafamidis, falls measures and a written plan.
R2: Not asking about carpal tunnel surgery. Bilateral carpal tunnel is a clue to transthyretin amyloid.
R4: Calling it ageing. A thick heart with low voltage and poor drug tolerance should make you think of amyloid.
R5: Asking only for an echo. Plasma cell tests and a pyrophosphate scan separate AL from ATTR.
R6: Adding blood pressure drugs. Conventional heart failure treatment is poorly tolerated here.
"Can I ask whether you have had carpal tunnel surgery?"
"A thick heart that doesn't tolerate drugs makes me think of amyloid."
"I'd like to check I've understood what worries you most."

ACC key points (2020) and ESC position statement (2021): keep a high index of suspicion in heart failure with preserved ejection fraction, especially when guideline-directed therapy is not tolerated; bilateral carpal tunnel syndrome is a common extracardiac sign of transthyretin amyloid.

Echo and cardiac MRI support an infiltrative cardiomyopathy but cannot confirm amyloid or its type. Evidence of a plasma cell disorder suggests AL, which needs urgent haematology, biopsy and mass spectrometry; AL with heart failure has a poor prognosis if treatment is delayed, so speed matters. Transthyretin amyloid: exclude a monoclonal protein first, then a bone-tracer (DPD or pyrophosphate) nuclear scan, then DNA sequencing if positive.

Conventional heart failure therapy is often poorly tolerated. Loop diuretics can cause hypotension and orthostasis. For transthyretin amyloid with cardiomyopathy, NICE recommends tafamidis (TA984, 19 June 2024; reduced deaths and cardiovascular hospitalisations against placebo) and permits acoramidis (TA1121, 14 January 2026) and vutrisiran (TA1115, 10 December 2025), each only under the NHS commercial arrangement, with the least expensive suitable option chosen after discussion with the patient; the amyloid centre starts them. Refer to a high-volume amyloid centre.
Macroglossia and periorbital purpura point to AL amyloidosis, not wild-type transthyretin amyloid.
THINK: HFpEF, intolerant of drugs, carpal tunnel: amyloid.
SAY: "A protein is stiffening your heart."
DO: Lying and standing blood pressure; ask carpal tunnel.
NUMBERS: Lying 118/70, standing 92/58 mmHg; breathless at rest; pyrophosphate scan strongly positive with no monoclonal protein (scenario values).
TRAP: More heart failure tablets.
FINISH: Free light chains and immunofixation, pyrophosphate scan, amyloid centre.

ACC (posted 5 November 2020; based on a JAAPA 2020 review). https://www.acc.org/Latest-in-Cardiology/ten-points-to-remember/2020/11/05/20/04/Cardiac-Amyloidosis Supports: Red flags, AL versus ATTR, diagnostic pathway and referral to a high-volume amyloid centre.

Diagnosis and Treatment of Cardiac Amyloidosis: ESC Position Statement. Eur Heart J 2021;42:1554-1568; ACC key points (April 2021). https://www.acc.org/Latest-in-Cardiology/ten-points-to-remember/2021/04/14/13/12/Diagnosis-and-Treatment-of-Cardiac Supports: exclude a monoclonal protein before a non-biopsy diagnosis of ATTR; pyrophosphate scan; referral to an amyloid centre.

NICE TA984. Tafamidis for treating transthyretin amyloidosis with cardiomyopathy (published 19 June 2024). Supports: tafamidis as an option for wild-type or hereditary ATTR cardiomyopathy within its marketing authorisation, under the commercial arrangement. https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ta984

NICE TA1121. Acoramidis for treating transthyretin amyloidosis with cardiomyopathy (published 14 January 2026). Supports: acoramidis as an option in the same population; use the least expensive suitable option after discussion with the patient. https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ta1121
